sourceNotes: Seeded from SEM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: SEM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: What it would cost to buy, as paid advertising, the same screen time a sponsor's marks earned inside a broadcast: qualified exposure seconds priced at that window's 30-second spot rate, then discounted roughly 25-50% because passive signage sells less than a commercial does.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-valuation roleplay asks whether a $400,000 rights fee paid off; you price the exposure seconds and apply the passive discount rather than quoting attendance.

terms.definition: The measurement rule that counts only branding a viewer could actually read — the logo must sit on screen unobstructed and in focus for at least one continuous second and fill a minimum share of the frame, or those seconds are struck from the valuation.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hand you an audit where gross on-screen time and qualified time differ by half; naming the threshold explains the gap instead of arguing the report is wrong.

terms.definition: How many dollars of promotional spending stand behind each dollar paid for the association itself; practice runs 1:1 at minimum and often 2:1, so a $500,000 rights fee needs another $500,000 to $1,000,000 before the partnership can work.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sponsorship-sale roleplay the client calls the fee affordable; you have to show the real budget is two to three times the fee or the signage sits unleveraged.

terms.definition: The uplift a property charges to lock every rival in one product class out of the venue, broadcast and apparel — the incremental fee less the revenue forgone by refusing the next-best buyer in that class, commonly 20-40% over the non-exclusive rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-pricing case gives you two soft-drink bidders; you must show exclusivity only pays when the premium beats what the excluded bidder would have spent.

terms.definition: Consideration delivered as goods, services or media instead of cash, credited against the rights fee at fair market value rather than list price — a $250,000 package carrying $100,000 of trade leaves $150,000 in cash, while the property books the trade at its own cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay sponsor offers product in place of money; the negotiation turns on valuing that trade at market before it may offset the fee.

terms.definition: Spreading a multi-year broadcast payment across the games actually telecast rather than evenly by calendar month, so a network carrying most of its schedule in one quarter recognizes most of that year's expense in that quarter.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-economics exam item asks why a broadcaster's fourth-quarter costs spike on a flat annual payment; the amortization pattern is the answer, not a fee increase.

terms.definition: A contract term barring a game's local telecast unless a stated condition is met — classically a sellout confirmed 72 hours before kickoff — inside a defined radius of the venue, shielding gate revenue from the broadcast of its own event.
terms.whyItMatters: A broadcast-rights roleplay asks whether to lift the local blackout; you weigh the walk-up ticket sales given up against the ratings and sponsor delivery the telecast adds.

terms.definition: Releasing one piece of content through exhibition channels in a fixed sequence, each protected by a contractual holdback of a set number of days before the next channel may carry it, with the price of each window falling as its exclusivity shortens.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-distribution roleplay asks about sending an event straight to streaming; the holdback lengths quantify the pay-per-view revenue that decision skips.

terms.definition: A network's promise that an advertiser's schedule will deliver a stated audience level, with any shortfall owed back in inventory computed as the guaranteed rating minus the delivered rating, multiplied by the units bought.
terms.whyItMatters: A sports-broadcast sales roleplay has a game under-deliver; you must state what the advertiser is owed and in what form before conceding a cash discount you do not owe.

terms.definition: The compensating commercial inventory issued when a guaranteed audience level is missed, valued at the original purchase rate rather than today's market rate and required to run in comparable dayparts so the replacement is genuinely equivalent.
terms.whyItMatters: When a rights-holder network under-delivers in a roleplay, the fight is over which daypart and which rate the replacement spots are valued at.

terms.definition: A per-subscriber monthly payment a distributor owes a broadcaster for carrying its signal: ten million subscribers at $2.50 each is $300 million a year, which is why a regional sports network is priced off subscriber count rather than ratings.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-rights case asks why a team's own channel is worth more than its advertising revenue suggests; the subscriber arithmetic carries the answer.

terms.definition: The licensee's payment computed on invoiced wholesale price after contractually allowed deductions — returns, freight and trade discounts, usually capped at a few percent — never on the retail shelf price, so 12% of a $30 wholesale unit is $3.60 and not $7.20.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandise-licensing roleplay quotes a rate without naming the base; pinning wholesale versus retail is the whole negotiation, because one percentage can pay double.

terms.definition: The upfront sum a licensor takes before any product ships is credited against royalties as they are earned, so a $100,000 advance at a 10% rate means the licensee owes nothing further until net sales pass $1,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: A licensing roleplay asks when the licensor next sees money; you compute the recoupment threshold instead of promising quarterly checks from day one.

terms.definition: Paid use of an amateur athlete's identity for endorsement, lawful only where it is genuine compensation for work rather than pay-for-play or a recruiting inducement, and reportable to the school — most policies require disclosure of any agreement at or above $600 within days of signing.
terms.whyItMatters: A collegiate-sponsorship roleplay dangles a booster-funded offer; the disclosure threshold and the inducement line decide whether you may sign it, not whether the athlete wants it.

terms.definition: A person's property interest in the commercial use of their identity, enforceable with no trademark or copyright behind it and surviving death in many states for a fixed term — seventy years in several — so an estate can still block an advertisement.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-licensing case puts a retired athlete's likeness on packaging; this doctrine and its post-mortem term are why clearance is required at all.

terms.definition: Royalties from products depicting several athletes are collected centrally and divided per unit among the players actually shown, so a card set featuring three athletes splits one royalty three ways rather than paying each of them a full rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A players-association roleplay asks how a team-wide trading-card deal pays out; the per-unit split, not individual star power, sets each athlete's check.

terms.definition: A termination right triggered by conduct bringing an endorser into public disrepute, where the drafted trigger decides everything: 'conviction' lets a brand act only after a verdict, while 'accusation' or 'public disrepute' lets it suspend payment on an allegation alone.
terms.whyItMatters: An endorsement-crisis roleplay hands you a headline with no charge filed; whether you may suspend the contract turns entirely on which trigger the clause uses.

terms.definition: Social-endorsement pricing benchmarked to audience size — roughly $10 per thousand followers per post, adjusted by measured engagement rate — so a 500,000-follower athlete posting at 3% engagement prices near $5,000, not at whatever the agent opens with.
terms.whyItMatters: An athlete-influencer negotiation roleplay starts from a number pulled out of the air; the follower-and-engagement math is how you defend or attack it.

terms.definition: A term stepping compensation up automatically once a defined objective achievement occurs — a major championship adding a set percentage to the annual retainer — as opposed to a bonus the brand may award at its own discretion.
terms.whyItMatters: A talent-contract roleplay tells you to hold the fee down; conceding an escalator rather than a higher base moves the cost into the year the win actually pays for.

terms.definition: The brand or studio owes the full contracted fee whether or not it ever uses the talent, unless it terminates inside a defined window before services begin — so shelving a campaign is a budgeting decision, not a saving.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-marketing roleplay kills a campaign after the spokesperson signs; this clause decides whether cancelling saves the client any money at all.

terms.definition: The revenue and price premium a franchise commands beyond what its market size and won-loss record predict — the residual once those are stripped out — which is why a losing team with deep support remains worth sponsoring.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-valuation case hands you two teams with equal attendance and opposite records; the residual, not the standings, says which audience a sponsor should buy.

terms.definition: Total campaign spend divided by net new full-season accounts — net of accounts lost over the same period — and judged against each account's renewal-adjusted multi-year value rather than one season's price.
terms.whyItMatters: A ticket-marketing roleplay calls a $300 acquisition cost too high; the renewal rate across three seasons decides whether it actually is.

terms.definition: A fan base's favorability toward a brand divided by the general population's, times 100 — a score of 140 means those fans are 40% more likely to favor it, and sponsors generally want above roughly 120 before paying a premium.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-sales roleplay demands proof the audience fits; the index score is the argument for charging above the rate card.

terms.definition: The guaranteed payment buying the association itself — the right to be called an official partner and to use the marks — separate from the money spent activating it and separate from any advertising bought around the event.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges test whether you can split the three budgets; quoting one blended 'sponsorship cost' loses the point every time.

terms.definition: A measured intensity tier — avid, casual or aware — built from attendance, media consumption and merchandise spend together rather than from ticket purchases alone, because the tiers convert to sponsor and premium offers at very different rates.
terms.whyItMatters: A fan-database roleplay asks who to target for a premium package; the avidity tier, not last season's buyer list, is what converts.

terms.definition: A perimeter around a host venue, set by ordinance for a defined window of dates, inside which signage, sampling and vending by non-sponsors is prohibited — the enforcement tool that makes paid exclusivity worth anything.
terms.whyItMatters: An event-sponsorship roleplay has a rival brand sampling across the street; whether you can stop them depends on the zone's boundary and its dates.

terms.definition: A period before rights reach open bidding in which the incumbent partner may negotiate alone, often paired with a matching right afterward, so a rival's bid can be topped rather than won outright.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-rights renewal roleplay asks why a competitor never got to bid; the window and the matching right are the whole reason.

terms.definition: Splitting the work of a SINGLE sale across different members — the customer configures and orders online, a local dealer installs and services, and the manufacturer invoices. It differs from dual distribution, where two COMPLETE channels each handle a whole sale end to end and therefore compete with each other for the same order.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selection roleplays for a product needing installation are scored on assigning each channel function to whoever performs it best rather than choosing one channel outright.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Varies price and allocates a fixed, perishable capacity across booking classes so the highest-paying demand can still be served late - airline seats, hotel rooms, rental cars. Dynamic pricing simply moves the number with demand, whereas here the binding constraint is capacity that expires worthless at a deadline and cannot be inventoried.
terms.whyItMatters: A lodging roleplay about a sold-out weekend expects the candidate to hold rooms back for late high-rate bookings instead of filling the house early at a discount.

terms.definition: Period sales divided by that period's seasonal index — 130,000 units in a month carrying an index of 1.30 is 100,000 on a level basis — and any trend line must be fitted to these adjusted figures, because fitting a line straight to raw seasonal data reads the busy season as growth that is not there.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast items hand monthly actuals alongside indexes and expect the adjusted series produced before any projection; skipping the division is the standard error that inflates a plan's growth claim and gets caught on the follow-up.

terms.definition: Makes an employer vicariously liable for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment even though the employer itself did nothing careless. A minor deviation from the route or task — a detour — stays inside that scope, while a substantial personal errand — a frolic — falls outside it, and a genuine independent contractor generally does not trigger the doctrine at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Agency roleplays about a delivery driver's crash ask whether the company pays, and the frolic-versus-detour line decides it.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: Placing the product in the customer's hands for a free trial, test drive or home-approval period and letting possession persuade, because giving the item back later registers as a loss. A takeaway close works from the opposite direction, threatening to withdraw the offer or the model rather than handing it over.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and automotive roleplays with a hesitant buyer reward a named trial-based close, and pairing it with the store's return policy shows you know the company's selling rules.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: The percentage used to convert a future dollar into today's dollars; raising it lowers the present value of every future cash flow and can flip a project from worth doing to not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the input that makes a net-present-value question answerable, and exam items test that a riskier project carries a higher one.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: A producer moving the same product through two channels that compete for the same buyer — company-owned stores alongside independent dealers, or a factory site priced against its own retail accounts. Courts judge the resulting squeeze on dealers under the rule of reason rather than treating it as automatically unlawful, so the legal exposure comes from how the two channels are priced, not from having both.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that adds a direct web store to an existing dealer network is graded on anticipating the dealer revolt and proposing price or territory rules that keep the arrangement defensible.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: An item deliberately priced at or below cost to pull traffic that then buys higher-margin goods. Roughly half the states police the tactic through unfair sales acts requiring a minimum markup over cost, often near 6% at retail, and it stays lawful because it lacks the recoupment intent that makes predatory pricing actionable.
terms.whyItMatters: Grocery and drugstore roleplays ask a candidate to defend a below-cost milk price to a judge who suspects the practice is illegal.

terms.definition: A document outlining a position's duties, qualifications, and reporting relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear descriptions guide hiring, set expectations, and reduce role confusion.

terms.definition: Divides a town's retail sales per resident by the state's retail sales per resident: 1.00 means locals spend exactly the statewide average at home, above 1.00 means the town is pulling shoppers in from outside its borders, and 0.80 means a fifth of local buying power is leaking to other towns.
terms.whyItMatters: Trading-area and site questions give local and statewide sales per person and expect the ratio plus a read on leakage; it is the figure behind arguing that a market is under-served and can support another store.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Sellers must re-scrub their calling lists against the federal registry at least every 31 days, and may reach a listed consumer only through an existing business relationship — 18 months after that person's last purchase, or 3 months after an inquiry — or with signed written permission. A list bought once and used for a year fails the scrub requirement no matter how it was sourced.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a purchase date and a call date and ask whether the relationship exemption still covers the call; a prospecting roleplay is scored on saying how often the list is cleaned.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: A strategy to make a product available in as many outlets as possible.
terms.whyItMatters: It maximizes convenience and market penetration for high-demand goods.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days, plus safety stock — the on-hand level that triggers a replenishment order, so it answers WHEN to order while economic order quantity answers HOW MUCH.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you daily usage, a supplier lead time and a buffer and ask at what stock level a buyer should place the reorder; picking the order size instead of the trigger level is the standard wrong answer.

terms.definition: Offers the components both individually and as a discounted package, so a buyer may take one piece alone or the whole set. Pure bundling removes the standalone option entirely, which extracts more from buyers who value the pieces evenly but loses every customer who wants only one of them.
terms.whyItMatters: Fast-food and software roleplays about a value meal or a suite ask which of the two forms fits a customer base with mixed preferences.

terms.definition: Compares an industry's share of local employment or sales with its share nationally — local share ÷ national share — so 1.0 marks a perfectly typical market, above about 1.25 says the activity is concentrated here and likely serves customers beyond it, and below about 0.75 says local demand is being met from somewhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: Situation-analysis questions supply local and national employment figures and expect the ratio read against 1.0; it is how a plan defends choosing one metro over another with evidence rather than preference.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: Total pay a rep receives at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus variable pay at plan, so a $60,000 base with $60,000 of commission at plan is $120,000 at a 50/50 pay mix. It is a plan figure and not a promise: only the base half is paid regardless of results, which is what separates it from a salary.
terms.whyItMatters: A recruiting roleplay that pitches a sales job is scored on explaining the split honestly, and quoting the total as if it were guaranteed is an ethical mark against you.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: The line of authority defining who reports to whom in an organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to escalate is a frequent judgment point in roleplays.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: GENUINE branded products sold through a channel the trademark owner never authorized, usually diverted from a market where the wholesale price was lower. They are lawful to resell in the United States because the first-sale doctrine exhausts the owner's control over that particular unit; counterfeit goods differ absolutely — those are fake, and selling them is trademark infringement no matter who bought them first.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-considerations items in channel management hinge on this split: a competitor undercutting an authorized dealer with real goods is generally legal, and the manufacturer's remedy is contractual, not a lawsuit for infringement.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: Relocating a business activity to another country while the firm still owns and runs it; outsourcing instead transfers the activity to an outside company that may sit in the same city, so the two axes are ownership and geography and a move can be one, the other, or both.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a firm opening its own support center abroad and expect the correct label, with 'outsourcing' as the planted distractor.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: A price reduction or payment a manufacturer gives a reseller in exchange for performing an advertising or display function - a co-op ad, an end-cap, a feature in the weekly circular. Robinson-Patman requires it be made available on proportionally equal terms to all competing customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-negotiation roleplays ask what the retailer owes in return for the money, and the answer is a performed service rather than simply a larger order.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring prior express written consent — signed, specific to marketing contact, and not made a condition of buying anything — before an autodialer or prerecorded message may call or text a mobile number, and requiring every seller to keep its own internal do-not-call list for five years. A checkbox buried in a purchase flow does not meet the standard.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-selling roleplay on texting a prospect list is graded on whether you ask how consent was captured; exam items contrast a consumer who bought something with one who signed a marketing permission.

terms.definition: Treatment group's response rate minus an untouched holdout group's rate, divided by the holdout rate: 6 percent against 4 percent is a 50 percent lift, and the 4 percent would have bought with no campaign at all. Without a holdout the campaign is credited with the whole 6 percent, which is how a coupon aimed at loyal buyers appears to work.
terms.whyItMatters: Judging whether a promotion actually caused sales, rather than coinciding with them, requires the untouched control group to be designed in before launch.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Buying a producer's goods legitimately in a low-price country and importing them for resale below the authorized dealer's price at home. The Supreme Court's 2013 ruling in Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons held that the first-sale doctrine covers copies lawfully made abroad, so the importer wins on copyright grounds and the producer's only real defenses are contract terms with its foreign distributors and genuine material differences in the product.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical- and legal-consideration questions in channel management use this case to separate what a manufacturer dislikes from what it can actually stop.

terms.definition: Binds a principal to a deal because the principal's own words or conduct led a third party to believe reasonably that the agent was authorized, even though no actual authority — express or implied — was ever granted. The manifestation must trace back to the principal, not to the agent's own claims, which is why an agent who simply asserts power creates none.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a terminated sales rep still carries company cards and signs an order tests this against actual authority.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Invoice terms granting a 2% discount if the bill is paid within 10 days, with the full amount due on day 30. Passing it up is costly: (2 / 98) x (365 / 20) works out near 37% a year, which is why forgone cash discounts are treated as one of the most expensive sources of short-term funds a business can use.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-terms roleplay asks whether to borrow in order to take the discount, and the annualized figure is what convinces the judge either way.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: The yearly percentage of assets a fund charges to operate, deducted from returns automatically so the investor never sees a bill for it.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two funds with identical holdings in an investment scenario comes down to this figure, since it compounds against the client every year.

terms.definition: Adding a product from a different category to the purchase — a case bought with a laptop — while upselling moves the customer up within the same line to a larger or higher-grade version of what they already chose. Suggestive selling covers both from the counter; the line that separates these two is category versus tier.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays scored on add-on sales ask you to name and demonstrate the technique, and calling a larger size a cross-sell is the error judges catch immediately.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: Resignations and retirements — separations the employee chose — divided by average headcount for the period, times 100: 18 quits against an average of 240 employees is 7.5%. Involuntary turnover uses the same denominator but counts terminations and layoffs the employer chose, and the two must be reported separately because the fixes differ: pay and management for one, hiring quality for the other.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that reports one blended turnover number is incomplete; the judge expects the voluntary share isolated before any retention spending is proposed.

terms.definition: Selling through a limited number of carefully chosen intermediaries in an area.
terms.whyItMatters: It balances accessibility with brand control and partner profitability.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: What the buyer actually owes after every trade, quantity and cash discount has come off the list figure. List price is the published starting point and the invoice price is what the seller bills before payment terms are applied, so all three numbers can differ on a single order.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing roleplays hand a competitor a list price plus a stack of discounts and ask what the check will actually be written for.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: Federal postal law lets anyone who receives goods they never ordered keep them as a free gift, with no duty to pay and no duty to ship them back, and a follow-up invoice creates no obligation. Only free samples plainly marked as such and merchandise sent by a charity asking for a donation fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items describe a company mailing a product with a bill attached and ask what the recipient owes; a customer-complaint roleplay expects you to tell the caller the item is theirs.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: Measures that protect confidential business and customer information from unauthorized access.
terms.whyItMatters: Good data security prevents costly breaches and keeps trust.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Codified at 17 U.S.C. section 109(a): once a copyright owner authorizes the first sale of a particular copy, its distribution right in THAT copy is exhausted, so the buyer may resell, rent or give it away without permission. Exhaustion covers distribution only — the reproduction right survives, so reselling a book is protected while photocopying it is not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the rule behind resale markets, used bookstores and outlet diverters, and channel exams test whether you know a manufacturer cannot use copyright to block resale of units it already sold.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: A series of trade discounts taken one after another off list: 30/20/10 means 70% of list, then 80% of that, then 90% of that, for a net factor of 0.504 rather than the 40% of list that adding the rates would suggest. These compensate channel members for functions performed, unlike a cash discount, which rewards only speed of payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesale-quote roleplays hand a competitor a stacked discount and ask for the net price, and adding the percentages together is precisely the error being tested.

terms.definition: Credential a private board grants after a psychometrically validated exam and keeps alive through periodic recertification, evidencing tested competence rather than legal permission. A certificate of completion is the near-neighbor that fools students: it is awarded merely for finishing a course, is never re-earned, and no board can revoke it.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on career-advancement resources ask which credential an employer will actually pay for; the answer is the one with an exam and a renewal cycle behind it.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: The reason a customer buys from this particular seller — service, location, reputation, staff knowledge or credit terms — as distinct from the product motive, which is the reason they want the item from anyone at all. A rep losing on patronage grounds cannot recover the sale by describing the product better.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior exam items sort a list of customer statements into the two motive types, and a roleplay customer who says a competitor is closer to home is testing whether you answer with service instead of features.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: Separating a business unit into an independent company by distributing its shares to existing shareholders, who receive no cash and simply hold two stocks instead of one; a divestiture sells the unit to an outside buyer and brings cash into the parent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which restructuring raises capital for the parent, and the tested distinction is that only the sale does while the share distribution does not.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Appointing only one or a few intermediaries to sell in a territory.
terms.whyItMatters: It gives partners strong incentives and control, ideal for premium products.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: A period's average value divided by the average across all periods, times 100, so a December index of 140 means that month runs 40 percent above a typical month and a February of 85 runs 15 percent below. Dividing actual sales by the index deseasonalizes the series, which is the only way a real trend can be told from the calendar.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay claiming sales collapsed from December to January is answered by deseasonalizing first, because the drop may be entirely the index and not a trend at all.

terms.definition: Rooms revenue / rooms available, which is the same as average daily rate multiplied by occupancy percentage. Because it charges the property for its empty rooms, it exposes the trade-off that ADR alone hides: a rate cut that fills the house can raise this figure even while the average rate falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about discounting a slow midweek are settled by comparing this metric against ADR rather than by looking at the room rate on its own.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: A selling arrangement in which silence counts as a yes — the seller announces the coming shipment and bills unless the buyer declines in time. It is lawful only if the buyer agreed to the terms up front, gets at least 10 days to reject each announced selection, and can cancel through a route as simple as the one used to enroll.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a book or subscription club and ask what makes the automatic shipment legal; a subscription-selling roleplay is scored on disclosing the cancellation route before the customer signs.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: The charter filed with the secretary of state that brings a corporation into legal existence, stating its name, registered agent, purpose and the number of authorized shares, and amendable only by shareholder vote plus another state filing. Bylaws are the separate internal rulebook — meetings, officers, quorum, notice — adopted by the board, never filed publicly, and changed without any state involvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A venture roleplay asks which document has to change before more shares can be issued to a new investor.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: An independent business that BUYS the goods, holds title, and therefore carries inventory risk, obsolescence and the credit exposure on resale, earning a margin rather than a fee. Agents and brokers sit on the other side of that line: they never take title, never bear the inventory risk, and are paid a commission — commonly 2 to 7 percent of the sale — for arranging the transaction.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a distribution partner and ask which type it is; the deciding fact is always whether title passed, and title decides who eats unsold stock.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: The nominal return minus the inflation rate — what an investment actually gained in purchasing power, which can be negative while the account balance rises.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a 2% savings account with 3% inflation and ask whether the saver gained; the account grew and the money bought less.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: The amount or percentage added to a product's cost to set its selling price.
terms.whyItMatters: Markup links cost directly to a pricing recommendation.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Guidance requiring any material connection between an endorser and a seller — payment, free product, a job, a family tie — to be disclosed clearly and right next to the claim rather than buried in a profile or behind a More link, and requiring a testimonial showing unusual results to state what a typical buyer should expect.
terms.whyItMatters: A social-selling roleplay that has you brief an influencer is graded on where the disclosure sits; exam items ask whether a free product with no cash payment still has to be disclosed, and it does.

terms.definition: Employees present at both the start and the end of a period, divided by the headcount at the start, times 100 — 190 of 200 starters still present is 95%. It is not simply 100 minus the turnover rate, because turnover uses average headcount and counts departures of people hired mid-period, while retention ignores anyone hired after the start date.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a turnover figure and ask for retention; subtracting from 100 is the trap, and the different denominators are the tested point.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: A paid matchmaker who brings a buyer and seller together for ONE transaction, takes neither title nor physical possession, and has no ongoing representation of either side once the deal closes. A manufacturers' representative differs on exactly that point: it works under a continuing contract for a defined territory and product line, calling on the same accounts year after year.
terms.whyItMatters: Food, real-estate and insurance channel scenarios turn on this: a broker cannot promise delivery terms or warranty support because it never owned the goods and has no standing agency.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: A measure of how much customer demand responds to a price change.
terms.whyItMatters: Elasticity predicts demand shifts and helps optimize price for revenue.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: Months a newly hired rep needs before carrying full quota, credited in steps — commonly no quota in the first quarter, half in the second and full in the third. A rep hired in March therefore contributes roughly a quarter of an annual number that year, which is why headcount added late almost never rescues a current-year gap.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items ask what revenue a mid-year hire adds this year, and the credit schedule is the whole answer; a roleplay on onboarding new sellers expects you to name the stepped quota rather than promise full production on day one.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: Mirrored pairs that are then striped: usable capacity is exactly half the raw total, so the same four 2 TB disks give 4 TB instead of 6, but the array survives one failure in every pair and rebuilds by copying a single disk rather than recomputing parity from all the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two quotes for the same four drives, the competitor has to trade 2 TB of capacity against a faster, safer rebuild — a judge expects the capacity figure said out loud.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: An orderly, methodical approach to tasks and decisions that follows a logical structure.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges favor structured reasoning over a scattered approach.

terms.definition: Disagreement between channel members over goals, territories, or profits.
