terms.whyItMatters: Conflict damages efficiency; resolving it is key to long-term channel health.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: The percentage of revenue left as profit after costs are subtracted.
terms.whyItMatters: Margin reflects pricing effectiveness against financial goals.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: A semi-autonomous division with its own mission, competitors, and profit responsibility, planned as if it were a standalone business inside the parent; it is the unit of analysis a portfolio matrix plots, which a functional department such as accounting can never be.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what is placed in the cells of a portfolio grid, and the tested error is plotting departments or individual products instead.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: The sales-tax duty a seller picks up in a state where it owns no building and employs no one, triggered purely by volume — commonly $100,000 of sales or 200 separate transactions into that state in the current or prior year. Cross the threshold and the seller must register, collect and remit there; a purely online business is not exempt.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce selling items give a state-by-state sales table and ask where tax must now be collected; an expansion roleplay expects you to raise registration before recommending a push into a new state.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: Written with dollar signs as $A$1, it pins both the column and the row so the address does not shift when the formula is copied down or across; a relative reference such as A1 moves with the copy, and a mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 freezes only the half carrying the dollar sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items give a tax rate in one cell and ask why copying the formula produced zeros further down the column; the missing dollar signs are the graded answer.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: The organized collection and analysis of information about markets, customers, and rivals.
terms.whyItMatters: Research helps a business understand needs before choosing tactics.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: A merchant wholesaler that owns the merchandise sitting on a retailer's fixture, chooses the assortment, sets the planogram, restocks on its own route, and is paid only for units that actually scan — so the retailer risks nothing but the floor space. A conventional wholesaler is the opposite arrangement: it bills the retailer at delivery and the retailer owns the unsold goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Convenience-store, greeting-card and paperback scenarios use this to test who bears shrink and markdown risk when the supplier still owns the stock on the shelf.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: Expresses the dollar markup as a percentage of what the merchandise cost the seller: (retail - cost) / cost. A $40 item ticketed at $100 carries a 150% markup on cost but only a 60% markup on retail; convert between them with markup-on-retail = markup-on-cost / (1 + markup-on-cost).
terms.whyItMatters: Merchandising math items hand a competitor one percentage and ask for the other selling price, and dividing by retail when the problem said cost throws off every later step of the calculation.

terms.definition: Forbids a director, officer, partner or agent from self-dealing, taking an opportunity that belonged to the enterprise, or competing with the principal, and a challenged transaction is judged on whether it was entirely fair rather than whether it was well reasoned. That standard is the split from the duty of care, where the business judgment rule shields an informed, disinterested, good-faith decision even when it turns out badly.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics roleplays about a manager steering a supply contract to a relative's firm are loyalty problems, not care problems.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: One deal's single commission pool divided between the rep who sourced it and the rep who closed it — 50/50, 30/70 or whatever the plan states — and the shares must total 100 percent. It changes who gets paid, never how much the company pays out, which is exactly the point students miss when they assume both reps earn a full commission.
terms.whyItMatters: Compensation items give a deal value, a commission rate and two named reps and check whether you double the payout; a team-selling roleplay expects you to settle credit before the sale, not after.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: The bit count of a cryptographic key, which cannot be compared across algorithm families: a 256-bit symmetric key doubles in strength with each added bit, while a 2048-bit RSA key rests on the difficulty of factoring and rates at only about 112 bits of equivalent strength. The far bigger number is the weaker key.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-security roleplay asks whether a supplier advertising 2048-bit encryption beats one advertising 256-bit; reading the digits alone gives the wrong recommendation.

terms.definition: The total annualized return on a bond held to the end of its term, counting coupon payments plus any gain or loss between purchase price and face value.
terms.whyItMatters: A bond bought below face value returns more than its stated coupon rate, and this is the figure that shows it in an investment comparison.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: A wholesaler that TAKES TITLE to a shipment but never physically handles it — it sells the load, then instructs the producer to ship straight to the buyer, collecting the margin between the two prices. That title-without-possession position is what separates it from a broker, which never takes title at all, and from a full-service wholesaler, which warehouses and delivers the goods itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Bulk-commodity channel questions test whether you see that this member is legally the seller of record and therefore liable on the sale, even though it never touched the freight.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: The process of orienting and integrating new employees into the organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong onboarding speeds productivity and conveys company values and procedures.

terms.definition: A plan for setting prices to meet business objectives and positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: A sound strategy is central to case presentations and positioning.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: A municipal rule making uninvited door-to-door solicitation of a home unlawful, so a canvasser needs a local permit or an invitation from the occupant before knocking. Courts have upheld these ordinances, and violating one is an offense in that town even when the product, the price and the sales pitch are all perfectly legitimate.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items place a canvassing crew in a town with such an ordinance and ask what must happen first; a field-selling roleplay expects permits checked before a neighborhood route is planned.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: Two different inputs producing the same fixed-length digest, which has to be possible because inputs are unlimited and digests are not. A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible outputs, but the birthday bound puts an attacker's expected work at about 2^128 attempts — the square root, not the full space — which is why a 128-bit digest is retired and a 256-bit one is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An information-ethics item asks why a system that stores digests instead of files can still be attacked; the square-root shortcut, not the digest length on the label, is the reasoning.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: A non-competing business that partners to offer complementary products to shared customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Affinity partnerships extend reach and value without adding intermediaries.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: Divides the same dollar markup by the selling price instead of by the cost: (retail - cost) / retail. It is the form buyers and merchandise plans quote, it always reads lower than the cost-based figure on the same item, and it converts back with markup-on-cost = markup-on-retail / (1 - markup-on-retail).
terms.whyItMatters: In a retail-buying roleplay a judge states margins the way the trade states them, so a candidate has to convert a vendor's quoted markup before comparing it to the store's own target.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: Plan language reversing commission already paid when the customer cancels or fails to pay inside a stated chargeback window — often 90 days for non-payment or the first 12 months of a subscription. Once that window closes the money is the rep's to keep, so the length of the window, not the cancellation itself, decides whether the company recovers anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics-and-compensation items ask what happens when a rep sells to a customer who churns in month two, and the answer depends on the window; a roleplay on writing a commission plan is graded on naming one.

terms.definition: Standard measure of non-degree instruction in which one unit equals 10 contact hours of participation in an accredited program, so a two-day 16-hour seminar earns 1.6 units. A college credit hour is a different currency entirely — roughly 15 contact hours across a semester — and licensing boards rarely convert one into the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked on the exam to price a training plan against a 40-hour renewal requirement, a competitor has to convert seminar hours into units before the budget makes sense.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged. The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: Performs the whole function set — carries inventory, extends trade credit, delivers, fields a sales force, and merchandises the account — and prices for it, typically working on a 15 to 25 percent gross margin. A limited-service wholesaler strips some of those out (cash-and-carry drops credit and delivery, a truck jobber drops credit) and consequently operates nearer 8 to 12 percent.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-cost questions ask why one supplier quotes a higher landed price than another; the answer is the bundle of functions inside the margin, not inefficiency.

terms.definition: A combination of firms in unrelated industries, pursued for earnings diversification rather than operating synergy; a horizontal merger joins direct competitors at the same stage, and a vertical merger joins a buyer with its own supplier or distributor.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items name the two merging firms' industries and ask for the merger type, because each type draws different antitrust scrutiny.

terms.definition: Petty and Cacioppo's two-route account of persuasion. An audience with both the motivation and the ability to think takes the central route, where argument quality decides and the resulting attitude is durable and resists counter-argument. An audience missing either one takes the peripheral route, where source attractiveness, the sheer length of the list and mood decide, and the attitude fades quickly. Adding more evidence for a distracted, uninvolved audience therefore changes nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A persuasive-message item that asks why a detailed cost-savings memo convinced the CFO but not the frontline staff is asking which route each audience was on.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: The retail convention of doubling delivered cost, so a $22 cost gets a $44 ticket. That one move is simultaneously a 100% markup on cost and exactly a 50% markup on retail, which is why the same practice gets quoted as two different percentages depending on the denominator.
terms.whyItMatters: Apparel and specialty-store pricing cases open with keystone as the starting ticket, then ask what margin survives after the item is marked down twice.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Split the population into internally similar subgroups, then draw at random inside every one of them, usually allocating each subgroup a share of the sample equal to its share of the population (n_h = n x N_h/N); cluster sampling looks similar but randomly picks a few whole groups and skips the rest entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: A sampling-plan roleplay that requires each store region to be represented in proportion is solved with strata, and the judge listens for the proportional allocation, not just the word random.

terms.definition: Under the UCC a seller sheds merchantability only with conspicuous language that actually uses the word merchantability, or with an as-is / with-all-faults notice, and sheds fitness for a particular purpose only in writing. An express promise once made cannot be disclaimed at all — fine print cannot cancel what the salesperson said out loud.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a spoken performance promise with an as-is sticker and ask which survives; a product-selling roleplay is scored on not making a claim the contract cannot later walk back.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: Continuing to fund a failing course of action in order to justify having chosen it. The dividing line from the sunk-cost fallacy is who is deciding: sunk cost is the reasoning error of counting unrecoverable spend at all, and anyone can make it, while escalation is the behavioral pattern driven by personal responsibility -- managers who personally picked the losing project invest substantially more in it than managers who inherited the same project.
terms.whyItMatters: The structural fix a judge is listening for in a case about a doomed store opening is handing the continue-or-kill call to someone who did not make the original decision; recommending only 'ignore what we already spent' answers the smaller half of the problem.

terms.definition: A court's decision to set aside limited liability and reach the owners' personal assets, available when the entity was run as a mere alter ego: personal and business funds commingled, formalities ignored, the firm deliberately undercapitalized at formation, or the corporate form used to work a fraud. Ordinary business failure never suffices — the owner has to have treated the corporation as a pocketbook.
terms.whyItMatters: Ownership-structure roleplays ask what an entrepreneur must actually do after incorporating to keep a house and savings out of reach.

terms.definition: The management of the flow of goods — storage, transportation, and delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Logistics efficiency drives channel cost, speed, and customer satisfaction.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Setting price by adding a standard markup to a product's cost.
terms.whyItMatters: It is a foundational method when a price must ensure cost recovery.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: What a sum invested today grows to by a stated date at a stated rate, computed forward with compounding rather than by adding equal yearly amounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-goal items give a monthly deposit and a rate and ask what the account holds in ten years; straight multiplication understates it.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: A tiered approval ladder capping how deep each level may cut price before escalating — a rep to 10 percent, a sales manager to 20, a vice president to 30, and anything past that to finance. Margin is protected by who is allowed to sign, not by how well an individual rep negotiates, so a buyer stalling for more has to be moved up the ladder.
terms.whyItMatters: A price-negotiation roleplay where the buyer demands 25 percent off is scored on whether you know you must escalate instead of conceding; pricing items test the ladder as a control on gross margin.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: Worker-days lost to unscheduled absence divided by (average number of employees times scheduled workdays), times 100 — 96 days lost across 40 employees over 20 workdays is 96/800, or 12%. Scheduled vacation and approved leave stay out of the numerator, which is why a business with generous paid time off can still post a low rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays ask you to quantify an attendance problem before proposing a policy; the ratio is what turns supervisor complaints into a defensible number.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: An independent salesperson carrying several producers' NON-COMPETING lines in a defined territory on commission of roughly 5 to 15 percent of net sales, with no title to the goods and no authority to set price or terms. A selling agent is the stronger form: it contracts for a producer's ENTIRE output and does hold authority over price, terms and promotion, effectively acting as that producer's marketing department.
terms.whyItMatters: A start-up roleplay choosing between hiring salespeople and appointing reps is graded on the fixed-versus-variable cost trade and on who controls pricing under each arrangement.

terms.definition: A classical four-question procedure for locating the exact point at which two sides disagree: conjecture (did it happen?), definition (what should it be called?), quality (how serious is it?) and policy (what should be done about it?). Arguing at the wrong level is the standard failure - answering 'what should we do' while the other side is still disputing whether anything happened produces two speeches that never touch.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge in a conflict roleplay disputes your facts and you answer with a solution, you lose points for never meeting the objection; this names the level you skipped.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: The percentage placed on goods when they first reach the floor, sized to absorb everything that will erode it: (operating expenses + profit + markdowns + employee discounts + shortages) / (net sales + markdowns + discounts + shortages). It is set deliberately higher than maintained markup because none of those reductions have happened yet.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-plan questions ask why a store tickets at 52% when it only expects to keep 40%, and the gap between this figure and maintained markup is the entire answer.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: An inquiry the sales team has formally accepted after confirming a named need, a budget owner and a decision timeline, where a marketing-qualified lead has cleared only a behavior score such as downloads or page visits. Handoff agreements usually give sales a fixed window, often 24 hours, to accept it or send it back with a stated reason.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel items ask at which stage marketing's responsibility ends and sales' begins; a roleplay on fixing a marketing-sales dispute is scored on defining the acceptance criteria and the return window.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by 365 — the same relationship as inventory turnover but expressed as days on hand, so it falls when turnover rises and 365 divided by turnover reproduces it.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a balance sheet and a cost of goods sold figure, exam questions ask how long a firm's stock sits before selling; answering with the turnover ratio when the item asked for days is a scored miss.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.
